clinical_category: Asthma self-management - individualized written action plan
blueprint_topic: Client education and escalation planning for asthma control and attacks
stem: A nurse reviews a written asthma action plan with a client. What is the primary purpose of the plan?

options.A: To give the client individualized instructions for routine control, worsening symptoms, and when urgent medical care is needed
options.B: To replace ongoing follow-up with the health care provider once asthma is stable
options.C: To delay use of prescribed reliever treatment until symptoms become severe
options.D: To use the same treatment steps for every person with asthma regardless of symptoms or provider instructions

rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance states that everyone with asthma needs an individual Asthma Action Plan created with a health care provider. The plan organizes actions according to asthma status, including what to do when doing well, when asthma is getting worse, and when there is a medical alert. Current NHLBI guidance likewise describes a written action plan as a provider-developed treatment plan that tells the client how to monitor and treat symptoms, which medicines to take and when, and when to call the provider or seek emergency care. B, C, and D contradict individualized asthma self-management and escalation planning.
educational_objective: Use a provider-developed written asthma action plan to guide individualized daily control, early response to worsening symptoms, and timely escalation for urgent or emergency care.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), corroborated by National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI/NIH)
source_document_title: Living with Asthma; Asthma - Treatment and Action Plan
source_version_date: CDC page dated 2026-05-04; NHLBI page last updated 2024-04-17; both current resources accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: CDC 'Living with Asthma' → 'Asthma Action Plans': everyone with asthma needs their own plan created with a health care provider; Green Zone, Yellow Zone, and Red Zone sections give actions for doing well, worsening asthma, and medical alert. NHLBI 'Asthma - Treatment and Action Plan' → 'Create an asthma action plan': the written treatment plan identifies triggers, how to recognize an attack and what to do, medicines and timing, when to call the provider or go to the emergency room, and emergency contacts.
source_claim_supported: Current federal guidance directly supports individualized written asthma action plans that translate current control or worsening symptoms into predefined treatment and escalation actions.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care client-needs subcategory (15–21% of items), within Safe and Effective Care Environment; this item tests coordinated client education, follow-up planning, and escalation of care.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The generic NHLBI homepage and over-specific threshold wording were replaced by current CDC 2026 asthma action-plan guidance, corroborated by NHLBI's current treatment/action-plan page. The final construct tests individualized treatment and escalation instructions without inventing universal medication doses or peak-flow thresholds.
audit_findings: The original source URL was generic and did not provide an exact action-plan locator.
CDC guidance dated May 4, 2026 directly states that every person with asthma needs an individualized action plan created with a health care provider.
The current CDC Green/Yellow/Red framework and NHLBI action-plan description directly support routine-control, worsening-symptom, and urgent-care instructions.
Universal medication doses and fixed peak-flow cutoffs were not made part of the keyed answer, avoiding unsupported precision across individualized plans.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct answer, no second defensible option, no cueing, no unsupported treatment threshold, and no unresolved conflict.
